forces.title: High energy and feedstock costs pressure UK chemicals sector
forces.description: The UK chemicals sector faces significant pressure from exceptionally high energy and feedstock costs. Wholesale gas prices rose 67% and crude oil surpassed $100 per barrel between February and March 2026. This creates a major cost disadvantage for domestic producers compared to competitors in the US and Middle East who benefit from cheaper resources. Coupled with weak global demand, overcapacity in basic chemicals, and low-priced imports, these cost pressures delay recovery and strain sector liquidity, hindering investment and competitiveness. Businesses must manage raw material exposure and preserve cash flow.

forces.title: Weak UK construction output dampens demand for building materials
forces.description: The UK construction sector is forecast to contract by 3.3% in 2026, a worsening trend from earlier predictions. This decline is driven by weakening confidence, rising financing and construction costs, and subdued investment. Specifically, private housing is expected to fall by 10.0% and repair, maintenance, and improvement activity by 8.0%. This directly impacts demand for construction materials, including cement, concrete, flat glass, ceramic tiles, and insulation. The persistent financial stress and insolvencies spreading across the construction industry will continue to exert pressure on material suppliers.

forces.title: Geopolitics and tariffs drive short-term metals price increases and stockpiling
forces.description: The metals sector is experiencing improved pricing and short-term trading conditions, primarily due to tariffs, quotas, and geopolitical events that have spurred stockpiling since February 2026. This has led to significant price increases, with some steel products rising by 40-50%. These protective measures are expected to support market conditions through the second half of 2026. While beneficial for immediate revenues, this front-loaded demand driven by anticipation of new quotas and import duties creates a risk of price correction once buying normalises. Businesses must manage inventory carefully to mitigate this potential downside.

forces.title: Rising costs for logistics, raw materials, energy impacting metals sector
forces.description: Despite improved short-term pricing, the metals sector faces significant headwinds from escalating costs. Higher expenses for logistics, raw materials, and energy are increasing financing and working-capital requirements for businesses. These cost pressures, alongside potential demand normalization after stockpiling, pose substantial challenges to financial stability. Exposure to import costs, construction demand fluctuations, and geopolitical disruption remain key credit considerations. Metals companies need to maintain pricing discipline and carefully manage their liquidity headroom and inventory levels to navigate this volatile environment effectively and preserve margins.

forces.title: Declining print demand and overcapacity weigh on paper sector
forces.description: The UK paper and print sector is burdened by declining print revenues, cost inflation, overcapacity, and insolvency pressures. Digitalization continues its long-term contraction of graphic paper demand, with internet penetration increasing to 93% in Europe. While packaging and specialty grades show more resilience, growth is selective. Competitive pressure from Asia's structural export platform exacerbates overcapacity in Europe, limiting price recovery. These combined factors create a high-risk profile for the sector, particularly for traditional print operators who face revenue erosion and squeezed margins amidst persistent cost increases.

forces.title: UK industrial deindustrialisation risk due to high energy prices
forces.description: Industrial energy prices in the UK are approximately 75% higher than the G7 average, severely undermining the competitiveness of UK-based energy-intensive industries, including chemicals and steel. This significant cost disparity increases the risk of deindustrialisation and the offshoring of emissions. From 2021 to 2025, nearly 30 chemical businesses in the UK closed, primarily citing uncompetitive energy costs, leading to a one-third fall in chemical output. This trend directly impacts job creation, investment, and the resilience of the UK's strategic industrial base, highlighting a critical need for affordable energy solutions.

forces.title: AI and automation boom drives demand for electronic chemicals and materials
forces.description: The accelerating adoption of AI, from machine learning to generative AI and robotics, is creating a significant tailwind for the electronic chemicals and materials segment. This boom cascades into demand for specialized inputs like photoresist, wet chemicals, thermally conductive adhesives, and engineered plastics used in microchips, memory, storage, and thermal management solutions for data centers. The market for these materials is expected to grow with CAGRs of 5-10% to 2030, offering high EBITDA margins exceeding 20% and attractive TSRs, making it a compelling focus area for chemical and materials companies.
forces.source_title: Reinventing the European pulp and paper operating model

forces.title: Concentrated critical mineral supply chains pose resilience risks for low-carbon technologies
forces.description: The global energy transition's reliance on critical minerals like lithium, cobalt, and nickel (for batteries), and graphite (for anodes), presents a significant resilience risk due to highly concentrated supply chains. For example, China supplies over 80% of global solar modules and more than 85% of the world’s battery cell production capacity by monetary value. This concentration creates vulnerabilities to geopolitical shocks, trade disruptions, and price volatility, potentially exceeding the gas-dependency challenges faced by Europe. Diversifying supply chains for these essential materials is crucial for ensuring the security and stability of low-carbon technology deployment.
forces.source_title: Investing in the energy transition: Time to look at whole-system value

forces.title: Sustainability shifts from differentiation to regulatory baseline for pulp and paper
forces.description: Sustainability in the European pulp and paper industry is transitioning from a consumer-driven differentiator to a baseline regulatory requirement. While the sector boasts recycling rates above 70%, investment in sustainability is now largely mandated by regulation rather than strong consumer pull, as willingness to pay more for eco-friendly products has weakened amidst macroeconomic uncertainty. This shift means that packaging purchasers face persistent barriers to adoption related to affordability, performance trade-offs, and regulatory uncertainty. Companies must integrate sustainability into their operating models to meet compliance, but its role in commercial differentiation is evolving.
forces.source_title: Reinventing the European pulp and paper operating model

forces.title: EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) raises import costs
forces.description: The EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which became operational in January 2026, converts embedded emissions into costs for imported goods such as steel, directly affecting landed costs and margins. This policy aims to reduce carbon leakage and align import costs with EU producers' ETS costs, making carbon intensity an explicit trade variable. CBAM requires robust, third-party verified emissions data, with conservative default values applied if data is unverified, potentially leading to significant overpayment. Companies face increased costs, supply chain pressures, and financial forecasting complexity due to evolving methodologies and carbon price volatility.
forces.source_title: CBAM: How companies can build from compliance to value creation

forces.title: Verified emissions data reduces CBAM costs and creates competitive advantage
forces.description: Companies that use verified emissions data for CBAM compliance can significantly reduce their carbon costs, potentially by 30-85% before decarbonization measures. This is because default values are intentionally conservative, and auditable footprints enable targeted actions to decrease carbon intensity. Early movers who establish robust monitoring, reporting, and verification (MRV) systems can gain a competitive advantage by providing credible product-level emissions data, allowing customers to minimize their CBAM liabilities. Active management of CBAM exposure through sourcing decisions, product redesign (e.g., lightweighting, higher scrap content), and financial mechanisms (e.g., hedging) allows firms to protect margins and secure advantaged supply.
forces.source_title: CBAM: How companies can build from compliance to value creation

forces.title: Supply chain constraints block aerospace and defense production targets
forces.description: Supply chain constraints are a critical obstacle, blocking deliveries in nearly 90% of aerospace and defense programs and hindering companies' ability to meet unprecedented demand. Production growth targets are 20-500% higher than recent levels, but backlogs signal an industry struggling to convert orders to output. This problem runs deeper than prime contractors can see, as lower-tier suppliers are forced to scale faster than any single customer's forecast indicates, creating bottlenecks. The high cost of industrial energy, materials, and labor also exacerbates these challenges, undermining UK aerospace growth and resilience.
forces.source_title: Aerospace and Defense: Winning the Race to Scale

forces.title: Defence sector shifts to resilience-led models, increasing critical materials scrutiny
forces.description: The UK defence sector is undergoing a fundamental shift from efficiency-led to resilience-led models, recognizing industrial capacity and supply chain depth as strategic assets. This necessitates a more deliberate approach to long-term investment, infrastructure, and workforce capability. Consequently, greater visibility across defence supply chains is now essential, requiring systematic assessment and management of exposure to critical materials, components, and technologies, particularly where supply is concentrated or vulnerable to disruption. This structural change demands a move from 'just-in-time' to 'just-in-case' industrial models, impacting material sourcing and production requirements.

forces.title: Chemicals value creation requires granular performance management across dispersed operations
forces.description: Value creation in the chemicals industry is highly dispersed across various parts of the value chain, including manufacturing sites, assets, product lines, and functions. This structural characteristic means that operational inefficiencies can easily go unnoticed, eroding value even if overall transformation metrics appear positive. To achieve consistent results, companies need granular performance management systems that provide transparency at the site, asset, product family, and customer levels. This requires integrating data from planning tools, control systems, and laboratory results into a common digital layer to optimize processes and make data-backed decisions faster and with greater precision.
forces.source_title: A dual transformation agenda for Europe’s chemicals industry

forces.title: European petrochemicals face feedstock disadvantage, leading to plant closures
forces.description: European polyethylene (PE) production, predominantly naphtha-based, faces a significant cost disadvantage compared to ethane-based production in NGL-rich regions like the US Gulf Coast and Middle East. Naphtha is globally traded and more expensive than locally abundant ethane, leading to raw material costs more than three times higher for naphtha-based systems. This feedstock competitiveness issue, coupled with higher capital costs and complex permitting, is causing a structural shift: up to five million tons of yearly capacity of existing European ethylene plants could be phased out over the next five years, with operators opting to import ethylene instead of reinvesting in integrated production.

forces.title: Global steel overcapacity compresses margins despite rising demand for low-carbon steel
forces.description: The global steel market continues to suffer from persistent overcapacity, with capacity exceeding demand by over 600 million tons in 2024. Much of this excess is in China, which has historically compressed margins for steel producers worldwide. While demand for low-carbon steel (e.g., from DRI-EAF technology) is growing in Europe due to decarbonization efforts and policies like CBAM, the overall global oversupply remains a significant headwind. This forces regions with higher production costs, like Europe, to rely on policy support and subsidies to make investments in cleaner technologies economically viable, rather than competing solely on cost.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: Low-carbon steel production driven by EU policies and energy costs
forces.description: The investment case for Direct Reduced Iron–Electric Arc Furnace (DRI-EAF) steel production is strengthening in Europe, driven by EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) carbon pricing and the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). These policies penalize high-emission Blast Furnace–Basic Oxygen Furnace (BF-BOF) production, making cleaner DRI-EAF more attractive. Although Europe faces higher natural gas and electricity costs compared to regions like Oman or the US, policy support and subsidies (e.g., in Germany) help overcome these disadvantages. This creates an opportunity for new low-carbon steel plants, with plans for 40-50 million tons of capacity by 2030, despite global overcapacity.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: UK industrial emissions decline due to closures and fuel switching
forces.description: Industrial emissions in the UK, particularly from iron and steel, refining, cement and lime, and chemicals (which collectively account for 50% of industrial emissions), have declined. This reduction is attributed to two main factors: the closure of some energy-intensive businesses, and a shift from higher-polluting coal and oil to natural gas and electricity in many facilities, alongside increased energy efficiency. While these changes contribute to meeting carbon budgets, the decline due to business closures reflects deindustrialisation, underscoring the challenge of achieving emissions reductions while maintaining industrial capacity and competitiveness in the UK.

viewpoints.title: UK chemicals sector under exceptional pressure from high costs and weak demand
viewpoints.description: The UK chemicals sector is experiencing exceptional pressure due to high energy and feedstock costs, weak global demand, and geopolitical instability. Output declined sharply in 2025, with conditions worsening in Q1 2026, driven by rising wholesale gas and crude oil prices. Domestic producers face a significant cost disadvantage compared to US and Middle Eastern competitors, whose energy and feedstocks are cheaper. Overcapacity in basic chemicals and competition from low-priced imports further delay a meaningful recovery, keeping sector liquidity under strain. Businesses should stress-test exposure and protect liquidity.

viewpoints.title: UK construction outlook weakened with significant declines in private housing
viewpoints.description: The UK construction sector's outlook has weakened, with total output forecast to contract by 3.3% in 2026. This downgrade reflects declining confidence, rising financing and construction costs, and subdued investment. Private housing and repair, maintenance, and improvement (RMI) activities are expected to see the sharpest declines at -10.0% and -8.0% respectively. While infrastructure remains resilient, a modest overall recovery of 1.2% is only forecast for 2027. Insolvencies remain elevated and are spreading to larger firms, indicating widespread financial stress across the sector.

viewpoints.title: UK metals sector benefits from pricing and improved trading, but financially fragile
viewpoints.description: The UK metals sector is experiencing better pricing and improved short-term trading conditions, partly driven by tariffs, quotas, and geopolitical events that encouraged stockpiling since February 2026. Some steel products have seen price increases of 40-50%, with protective measures expected to support conditions through H2 2026. However, the sector remains financially fragile, and Europe generally lags other regions. Higher logistics, raw-material, and energy costs are increasing financing and working-capital requirements. There is a risk that demand and prices could correct once stockpiling normalizes, necessitating careful inventory management.

viewpoints.title: UK paper and print sector faces high risk, packaging subsector more resilient
viewpoints.description: The UK paper and print sector carries a high-risk profile, with significant variations across subsectors. Packaging demand and sustainability-led opportunities offer support, indicating resilience in these areas. However, declining print revenues, persistent cost inflation, overcapacity, and insolvency pressures continue to weigh heavily on the overall market. Credit quality is becoming increasingly polarised, with packaging-focused and technologically advanced businesses proving more resilient than traditional print operators. Businesses need to assess counterparties by subsector and business model, as the gap between stronger and weaker operators will likely remain pronounced.

viewpoints.title: Domestic energy supplies underpin UK manufacturing competitiveness and strategic industries
viewpoints.description: OEUK highlights that the UK’s offshore energy sector, beyond powering homes and businesses, fundamentally underpins the competitiveness of the manufacturing base. It supports strategic industries like chemicals, steel, and advanced engineering, and provides essential feedstocks for critical products such as medicines, fertilisers, and materials vital for the energy transition. Affordable, secure, and reliable energy is considered the foundation for modern industrial economies. Maintaining domestic energy production is crucial for national security, preventing an increased reliance on imports, and sustaining economic value and jobs within the UK.

viewpoints.title: Electronic chemicals and materials offer compelling growth opportunity in AI infrastructure boom
viewpoints.description: Electronic chemicals and materials are identified as a compelling growth area for chemicals, petrochemicals, and materials companies, driven by the accelerating demand for AI and automation. This segment is expected to see CAGRs of 5-10% to 2030, with EBITDA margins consistently exceeding 20%. The growth is spurred by the need for specialized chemicals (e.g., photoresist, wet chemicals, thermally conductive adhesives) in semiconductor manufacturing, data centers, and robotics. High R&D, long qualification cycles, and strong supplier-customer integration create significant barriers to entry, leading to 'sticky' relationships and attractive returns.
viewpoints.source_title: Opportunities for Chemical Companies in the AI Infrastructure Boom

viewpoints.title: European pulp and paper industry faces structural pressures requiring transformation
viewpoints.description: The European pulp and paper industry is at a decisive point, facing weaker demand, rising costs, and growing competition. Long-term trends like demographic shifts and digitalization are reshaping demand, particularly for graphic paper. Structural pressures include volatile input costs (pulp, wood, energy), global competitive intensity, and a shift towards regulation-driven sustainability rather than consumer pull. Performance depends increasingly on operational agility and productivity, as demand growth alone cannot offset underperformance. Companies need to accelerate transformation to remain competitive and capture future value, focusing on integrated operating models and commercial discipline.
viewpoints.source_title: Reinventing the European pulp and paper operating model

viewpoints.title: Top chemical transformations balance performance improvement with radical reshaping
viewpoints.description: The strongest transformations in Europe’s chemicals industry achieve significantly greater impact by setting ambitious goals that combine near-term performance improvement with radical reshaping of portfolios, operations, and capital allocation. These transformations are led by CEOs who commit meaningful resources and attention, moving the agenda from the boardroom to granular, line-owned initiatives across the value chain. Success hinges on execution discipline, building a performance management system that links ambition to operational drivers of value, site by site. This approach allows companies to improve current performance and fund future strategic priorities with greater confidence and control.
viewpoints.source_title: A dual transformation agenda for Europe’s chemicals industry

demand_drivers.description: The chemicals sector supplies critical inputs to diverse industries including pharmaceuticals, defence, energy, aerospace, automotive, food production, water treatment, and clean technologies, making its economic contribution widespread.

Chemicals are vital for national resilience, underpinning healthcare, defence, critical infrastructure, and water security, while also providing essential inputs for manufacturing supply chains. It also enables net-zero transition technologies.

pnl_drivers.description: The sector's substantial export contribution (15% of UK exports) is a key revenue driver, but its competitiveness is vulnerable to domestic energy and feedstock costs.
Supporting nearly 500,000 jobs across the economy highlights its broad economic value, but deindustrialisation due to high costs risks job losses.

market_sizing.methodology: The UK chemicals sector contributes £61 billion in annual exports, representing around 15% of total UK exports, and supports approximately 500,000 jobs across the wider economy.

demand_drivers.description: Accelerating demand for AI (including generative AI, copilots, multimodal systems) and robotics drives the need for specialized electronic chemicals and materials integral to manufacturing microchips, memory, storage, and other electronic devices.
The shift to advanced node technology in microchips requires more materials, and expanding electronics manufacturing globally (including Asia, US, EU) fuels demand.

pnl_drivers.description: The electronic chemicals and materials segment delivers high EBITDA margins, consistently exceeding 20%, driven by specialized, high-value applications and barriers to entry.
The segment delivered a median annual TSR of 15% from 2020 through 2024, outperforming the global chemicals industry (7%) and all industries (10%).

new_opportunities.description: Successful investment involves strategically acquiring companies in niche markets, leveraging existing capabilities, co-developing with customers, and scaling through disciplined M&A and investment to exploit high barriers to entry and 'sticky' customer relationships.

market_sizing.methodology: The total addressable market (TAM) for electronic chemicals and materials across the semiconductor supply chain is estimated to be over $75 billion today. This market is experiencing accelerated growth driven by increasing demand for AI and automation technologies.
market_sizing.source_title: Reinventing the European pulp and paper operating model

demand_drivers.description: Demand for polyethylene is closely tied to global population growth and increasing urbanization, particularly in emerging economies where consumption of plastic products is expanding.

Polyethylene is a foundational input in modern economies, widely used in packaging, construction materials, medical devices, and industrial products, linking its demand directly to consumer goods consumption.

market_sizing.methodology: Global installed capacity for polyethylene (PE) production is roughly 150 million metric tons per year. Demand grew approximately 3% annually before 2020, slowed to 1-2% in recent years, but long-term scenarios project a rebound to about 3% annual growth, reaching 200 million metric tons annually by 2035. Meeting this demand would require 10 to 25 new world-scale crackers.

demand_drivers.description: The push for lower CO2 emissions, particularly driven by EU ETS and CBAM, increases demand for low-carbon steel production methods like EAF and DRI-EAF as alternatives to traditional BF-BOF technology.
Supportive policies and heavy subsidies in regions like Germany facilitate investment in DRI-EAF plants, despite higher underlying costs in some European locations, driving new capacity.

new_opportunities.description: Significant investment in new EAF and DRI-EAF plants across Europe presents an opportunity to capture value from the transition to lower-emission steel, driven by increasing carbon pricing and regulatory incentives.

market_sizing.methodology: Plans are underway in Europe for more than 17 Electric Arc Furnace (EAF) and Direct Reduced Iron–EAF (DRI-EAF) steel plants, projected to produce approximately 40 to 50 million metric tons of low-carbon steel by 2030.
market_sizing.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace
